passage:
Dear Varun Chetta,
You asked on the phone why I sound so flat. I'll try to answer here, because writing is easier than saying it.
For about three months I've been waking at four with my heart racing, dreading school. I haven't told anyone, for a whole list of reasons. Achan says counsellors are for people who can't manage their own minds. I worry it costs a lot, and Amma is already counting every rupee. Mostly, I tell myself it isn't bad enough. I still go to class. I still smile in photos.
But a senior at school waited until she couldn't leave the house at all. I don't want to wait that long.
Our school counsellor is free. When you're home next Saturday, will you come with me, and help me tell Amma and Achan?
Gopika

qa.q: At what time has Gopika been waking up?
qa.a: At four, with a racing heart.
Gopika is afraid Achan will see it as weakness, worries about the cost for Amma, and thinks it isn't bad enough.

qa.q: What choice does Gopika make at the end of the letter?
qa.a: To ask early: Gopika asks Varun Chetta to come to the free school counsellor and help tell Amma and Achan.

qa.q: How might Varun Chetta feel reading this letter?
qa.a: He may feel worried but glad to be trusted, and able to make the first step less frightening for Gopika.

grounding: It shows a teenager held back by fear of seeming weak, cost, family reaction and feeling it is not bad enough, who decides to ask for help early.

passage: Jahnavi, since this podcast is about asking for help, here's why I waited so long. I'm Farida, and I kept a list of excuses. First: people would call me weak. In our class, anyone who cried was a joke for weeks. Second: my parents already work double shifts, and I thought a counsellor would cost money we didn't have. Third, the big one: it wasn't bad enough. Other people had real problems. So I waited. In Class 10 I stopped sleeping properly, then stopped reading, which I used to love, then stopped answering my friends. By the time I told our sports teacher, I'd missed a whole term. She listened, took me to the school counsellor that same afternoon, and it turned out the service was free. If I could talk to the Class 10 me, I'd say: the day you start making excuses is the day to ask.

qa.q: Why did Farida believe it "wasn't bad enough"?
qa.a: Farida felt unsure her struggle counted, since other people had real problems, so asking for help seemed unjustified.

qa.q: What did waiting cost Farida, and what choice would Farida make now?
qa.a: Farida missed a whole term; now Farida would ask for help as soon as the excuses start.

qa.q: How might the sports teacher have seen Farida's decision to speak up?
qa.a: The teacher would likely see it as brave and act quickly, taking Farida to the counsellor that same afternoon.

grounding: It shows a teenager who delayed asking for help out of fear of seeming weak, worry about cost and feeling it was not serious enough, and learned to ask early.
